The clock said 11:55. Santosh's finger hovered. "She checked out at the end," he muttered, and clicked 2 anyway. The page loaded: Submitted.

In the college library in Bengaluru, Devika opened the feedback form for Manjula ma'am's urban design elective. The last three weeks had been a blur of rushed slides and a surprise assignment, and Manjula ma'am had seemed tired and short with everyone.
Devika typed fast: "Disorganised. Stressful. Would not recommend." She gave it two stars.
Her friend Swara leaned over. "Wait, isn't this the course with the heritage walk? You said it was the best day of the year."
"That was ages ago. In August."
"And the guest architect? And the model-making weeks?"
Devika looked at the screen. She did remember the walk, the old stepwell, the sketching. But it felt like a different course. The stressful weeks felt like the real one. She left the two stars.

qa.a: "Disorganised. Stressful. Would not recommend."

qa.a: The rushed slides and surprise assignment are the most recent memories and still feel sharp, so August's heritage walk seems far away, like a different course.

qa.q: How could Devika make her feedback fairer?
qa.a: List the course week by week, the walk, the guest architect and the model-making as well as the rushed end, and rate the whole, while still mentioning the stress.

I'm Yash, and last year I gave Aadhya a 2 out of 5 in our final-year project peer rating. I still think about it.
We were a team of four building a water-quality sensor for the college lake. From August to February, Aadhya did most of the real work. She wrote the code, fixed the sensor when it fried, and stayed late when the rest of us went home.
Then in March her grandmother fell ill and she went home to Nagpur for the last two weeks. The rest of us rushed the report and the demo. When the rating form came, all I could see was those two weeks: her empty chair, the late nights we did without her.
Two, I typed. Missed the final phase.
In May I scrolled back through our group chat to find a file, and it was all her messages. Month after month.

qa.a: Yash gave Aadhya a 2 out of 5.

qa.q: Why did a 2 feel fair to Yash when filling in the form?
qa.a: The last two weeks without Aadhya were the freshest and most stressful memory, so her empty chair crowded out the six months when she did most of the real work.

qa.q: What could Yash do before rating a teammate next time?
qa.a: Yash could look back over the whole project, for example by scrolling the group chat or listing each month, before letting the final weeks decide the score.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when she sees a 2 after carrying the project for months?
qa.a: Aadhya would likely feel hurt and unfairly judged, especially since she was away for a family reason and had done most of the work before that.

grounding: It shows a student rating a team member mostly on the last few weeks, so recent absence dominates the overall impression.

Course coordinator's note, end-of-semester feedback (Kishore)
Ujjwal, 20, gave our twelve-week pottery workshop 1 out of 5, with the comment: "Badly run, rushed, room was unbearable."
The last two weeks were hard. The fan in the studio broke, and we squeezed two sessions into one to finish before exams. His complaint about those weeks is fair.
But in his mid-semester form, Ujjwal wrote: "Best class I've taken. I look forward to it every week." He made eleven pieces, more than anyone, and brought his cousin to the open studio in week 6.
I met him and showed him both forms side by side. He read them, laughed a little, and said, "Honestly I only remembered the heat."
Next: we'll collect short feedback every three weeks, so the final form isn't just the last fortnight, and the fan is being repaired.

qa.q: What score did Ujjwal give the pottery workshop?
qa.a: He gave it 1 out of 5.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's comment "I only remembered the heat" suggest about how he judged the course?
qa.a: It suggests the uncomfortable last two weeks felt like the whole course to him, pushing aside the weeks he enjoyed and the eleven pieces he made.

qa.q: Which step by Kishore helped, and why?
qa.a: Showing Ujjwal both forms side by side, so he could see his own earlier praise and notice how much the last weeks had coloured his rating.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel reading the 1 out of 5?
qa.a: Kishore may feel stung, since he knows how much Ujjwal loved the class for most of the term, while also accepting that the last weeks were genuinely hard.

grounding: It shows a student rating a course almost entirely on the last few weeks, so recent problems dominate the overall impression.
